paragraphs.text: Ode didasealiea Asaphi. The six first verses are proemial, wooing attention from the dignity, difficulty, antiquity, certainty, &c., of the matter in this psalm discoursed on, containing an abstract of the whole Pentateuch, and acquainting us with the ancient way of preaching, which was a historical narration of the miraculous mercies that God had from time to time conferred upon his people, their hateful abuse of his benefits, and their punishments thereupon. This is to be seen in various psalms, in St Stephen’s sermon, Act 7:1-60, and St Paul’s, Act 13:1-52, et est sane valde venerandum istud sanctae antiquitatis monumentum, This is a very venerable monument of holy antiquity, and teacheth us the right use of history, quae dicta est παρα το ισταναι τον ρουν, saith Plato.
paragraphs.anchor: Maschil of Asaph

paragraphs.text: i.e. To my doctrine, which hath its name in Hebrew from darting it into the soul; and these are the psalmist’s words in God’s name, calling for utmost attention.
paragraphs.anchor: Give ear, O my people, to my law

paragraphs.text: Lay them close to my lips, that no parcel of this sacred language fall to the ground by your default. Eνωτιζεσθε, Aurizate, auribus haurite, Receive it into your ears; yea, draw up the ears of your mind to the ears of your bodies, that one sound may pierce both, Act 2:14 Isa 55:3. "Hear, and give ear; be not proud; for the Lord hath spoken it," Jer 13:15.
paragraphs.anchor: Incline your ears, &c.

paragraphs.text: I will speak freely and plainly (I will open my mouth, Mat 5:2 Act 10:34), and yet acutely and accurately. See Psa 49:4, {See Trapp on "Psa 49:4"}
paragraphs.anchor: I will open my mouth in a parable

paragraphs.text: Heb. I will well out (as from a spring or fountain) dark or sharp sayings, transacted and recorded of old, but of good use for ever. Difficulty doth not discourage, but rather whet on heroic spirits to a more diligent inquiry. Aben Ezra noteth here, that Psa 78:9, "The children of Ephraim," &c., is a parable, and Psa 78:25, "Man did eat angels’ food," is a riddle, or dark saying.
paragraphs.anchor: I will utter dark sayings of old

paragraphs.text: Hearing and seeing are the two learned senses, whereby knowledge, yea, life, entereth into the soul, Pro 2:2; Pro 2:10 Isa 55:3.
paragraphs.anchor: Which we have heard and known

paragraphs.text: Have delivered down to us from hand to hand, whetting upon us the written word, Deu 6:7, and adding thereunto, for explication, many other things fit to be known.
paragraphs.anchor: And our fathers have told us

paragraphs.text: The manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit with, 1Co 12:7, neither is any one born (much less born again) for himself; but must be as useful as may be in his generation,
paragraphs.anchor: We will not hide them from their children

paragraphs.text: Paulum sepultae distat inertiae
Celata virtus - (Hor.).
The praises of the Lord] The praise worthy acts of God for his people, and against their enemies; for these two are not sundered, Php 1:28.

Lest any should attribute too much to ancient traditions, and to show that antiquity must have no more authority than what it can maintain; the psalmist here (as afterwards the prophet Isaiah) calleth them to the law and to the testimonies; for if any speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them, Isa 8:20.
paragraphs.anchor: For he established a testimony in Jacob, &c.

paragraphs.text: i.e. Succeed their parents both in their place and office of teaching their posterity; not suffering the truth which is after godliness {Tit 1:1} to fail and fall in the streets, Isa 59:14-15, or if it do, raising it up again, and restoring it to their utmost.
paragraphs.anchor: Who shall arise and declare them

paragraphs.text: Summa legis divinae et scopus, this is a brief of the Bible, viz. to believe in God and obey his law; both which men shall the better do, if they forget not his works.
paragraphs.anchor: That they might set their hope in God

paragraphs.text: Fathers are not always to be followed, Eze 20:18-19. He zealously affected his fathers, but not well, who said, I will follow them sicut bos armentum, etiamsi ruant, though I fall with them (Cicero Epist.).
paragraphs.anchor: And might not be as their fathers

paragraphs.text: Aver satrix et irritatrix.
paragraphs.anchor: A stubborn and rebellious generation

paragraphs.text: Double-minded men, unstable in all their ways, Jas 1:8, having religionem ephemeram, as Beza said of Baldwin, that Ecebolius II.
paragraphs.anchor: A generation that set not, &c.

paragraphs.text: As was that martyr’s who said, Though you may pluck the heart out of nay body, yet you shall never pluck the truth out of my heart. The heavens shall sooner fall, said another, than I will forsake the truth I have once received.
paragraphs.anchor: And whose spirit was not stedfast with God

paragraphs.text: This the Rabbis interpret of eight thousand Ephraimites, who would needs break prison, as it were, out of Egypt (before the time that God had set for their deliverance thence), and seize upon Palestine, the promised land; but with evil success; for they were slain by the men of Gath, to the great grief of their father Ephraim, 1Ch 7:21-23, and to the increase of their servitude in Egypt, Exo 1:8-14 This is historia Caballica. See R. Solomon on those words, Exo 15:14, the people shall hear and be afraid; sorrow shall take hold on the inhabitants of Palestina, who, remembering what a slaughter they once made of these Ephraimites, shall fear the just revenge of that cruelty. Others interpret this text by Jdg 1:29, and some by 2Ki 17:1-18, with Hos 10:6-8, &c., but this to me seemeth most likey. These are ancient things, and of such the psalmist promiseth to treat, Psa 78:2-3.
paragraphs.anchor: The children of Ephraim being armed, &c.

paragraphs.text: Trusting to their own strength and warlike preparations, and choosing rather to be counted temerarious than timorous.
paragraphs.anchor: Being armed and carrying bows

paragraphs.text: Carnal confidence seldom comes home otherwise than weeping.
paragraphs.anchor: Turned back in the day of battle

paragraphs.text: And so betrayed themselves into the hands of divine justice, they were worthily worsted. See 2Ch 15:2.
paragraphs.anchor: They kept not the covenant, &c.

paragraphs.text: They were set upon it, and would not be ruled by their father Ephraim, or any other that counselled them to the contrary; and haply said the like to them that Archidamus did to his too daring son, Aut viribus adde aut animis adime, Either add to thy forces or abate of thy courage.
paragraphs.anchor: And refused to walk in his law

paragraphs.text: Forgetfulness is a grave; et ingrato quicquid donatur, deperditur, all is lost that is conferred on an ungrateful person.
paragraphs.anchor: And forgat his works, and his wonders

paragraphs.text: Whereof they were eye-witnesses, and therefore could not plead ignorance or excuse. The Hebrew hath it, a marvel, or a miracle, collective.
paragraphs.anchor: Marvellous things did he, &c.

paragraphs.text: Corruptly called afterward Tan and Tanis; a populous and principal city of Egypt even in Isaiah’s time, Isa 19:11-13; about 23 miles from Memphis, saith Josephus: there Moses wrought his miracles (Ptolemy. Strabo).
paragraphs.anchor: In the field of Zoan

paragraphs.text: Making it fordable for them, and fixing those fluid waters, like stone walls, on each hand of them, while they passed through with ease and safety. Every main affliction is our Red Sea; which, while it threatens to swallow, preserveth us.
paragraphs.anchor: He divided the sea

paragraphs.text: This cloud not only conducted them, but also compassed them in on every side, both to keep them from the parching heat of the sun, and to save them from the sight and violence of their enemies, Exo 13:21. A figure of God’s guidance of his Church, and protection over the same, Isa 4:5 Neh 9:9.
paragraphs.anchor: In the daytime also he led them with a cloud

paragraphs.text: And set them abroach, both that in Rephidim, Exo 17:1-8, and the other in Kadesh, Num 20:1-13 Moses Nehamides, on Exo 17:1-8, saith, that the old Jewish doctors held that the rock of Rephidim not only yielded waters like a river all those forty years wherein they were in the wilderness, but followed them also there whithersoever they went. This agreeth well with that of the apostle St Paul, 1Co 10:4, who sweetly allegorizeth this history.
paragraphs.anchor: He clave the rocks

paragraphs.text: i.e. In great abundance, Ad satietatem usque. Rocks sooner yield fire than water; but what cannot God do?
paragraphs.anchor: As out of the great depths

paragraphs.text: Idem enuntiat per Epexegesim, ad miraculi magnitudinem ostendendam. The same again, to set forth the greatness of the miracle. This was a standing miracle, as was also the pillar of cloud, the pillar of fire, and the manna.
paragraphs.anchor: He brought streams also out of the rock

paragraphs.text: The better he was to them the worse were they toward him, as if God had hired them to be wicked; and this was ordinary with them, and is still among us. Oh the Divine patience!
paragraphs.anchor: And they sinned yet more against him

paragraphs.text: In terra arida ubi Deo indies indigebant, ibi peccabant, saith Aben Ezra here. This was another aggravation of their sin.
paragraphs.anchor: By provoking the most High in the wilderness

paragraphs.text: In their hearts first, but afterwards also with their lips. The psalmist here striketh at the root of their wickedness.
paragraphs.anchor: And they tempted God in their heart

paragraphs.text: Not for their necessity (that had been more excusable, Pro 6:30), but to satisfy their inordinate appetite, to gratify their licorish palate.
paragraphs.anchor: By asking meat for their lust

paragraphs.text: Their villanous and foul thoughts blistered and brake out at their lips.
paragraphs.anchor: Yea, they stake against God

paragraphs.text: This was a blasphemous question. God can do more than he will; but whatsoever he will do shall be done, and nothing can hinder it. "Lord, if thou wilt, thou canst make me clean," said he in the Gospel. And this was better than that of the other, who said, "If thou canst do any thing, help us," Mar 9:22
paragraphs.anchor: Can God furnish a table?

paragraphs.text: And so showed his power; we cannot deny it; but now for his will.
paragraphs.anchor: Behold, he smote the rock, &c.

paragraphs.text: They should have said, Will he serve our lusts? but that they were ashamed to say.
paragraphs.anchor: Can he give bread also?

paragraphs.text: i.e. Dainty and delicate flesh, such as is that of quails, meat for a king; for they carried their cattle out of Egypt with them; and so they could not be without ordinary flesh, too good for such unthankful miscreants.
paragraphs.anchor: Can he provide flesh for his people?

paragraphs.text: Efferbuit, excanduit. Anger is a kind of fire, a boiling of the blood about the heart, through desire of revenge. "But fury is not in me," saith God, Isa 27:4. If anger be ascribed unto him, as here, it is an expression fitted to our apprehension, because he doeth that which angry men use to do, viz. chide and smite for sin; but all in a way of justice, and without the least perturbation.
paragraphs.anchor: Therefore the Lord heard this, and was wroth

paragraphs.text: It began to smoke and burn.
paragraphs.anchor: So a fire was kindled

paragraphs.text: Ascended, i.e. Flamed, for anger beginneth at the heart, and then cometh up into the brain, face, nostrils.
paragraphs.anchor: And anger also came up

paragraphs.text: As faith is a radical and complex grace; so is unbelief a radical sin, a teeming vice, Heb 3:12, a wellspring of wickedness; many sins are bound up in it, as Cicero saith of parricide.
paragraphs.anchor: Because they believed not in God

paragraphs.text: i.e. In his saving promises.
paragraphs.anchor: And trusted not in his salvation

paragraphs.text: Though he had served them as never prince was served in his greatest state, yet all served not turn.
paragraphs.anchor: Though he had commanded the clouds

paragraphs.text: Rupturas nubium, raining down upon them plenty of manna; so that it was not hunger, but humour, that set them a lusting.
paragraphs.anchor: And opened the doors of heaven

paragraphs.text: Manna signifieth, What is this? whereunto in the allegory answereth, This is my body. Or, according to others, it signifieth a prepared portion, prepared by God, so that they might presently eat of it, though they might grind, or pound, or bake, or boil it also, they might do anything with it, as they might with meal; whence it is here called the corn of heaven, that is, a seed which was unto them instead of corn.
paragraphs.anchor: And had rained down manna upon them

paragraphs.text: Man did eat angels’ food] Heb. the bread of the mighty, Pan de nobles (Hispan.); (Angels are called mighties, Isa 10:34 Rev 18:21); such delicate bread as might beseem angels to eat, if they did eat any at all; such as the poets feign to be their Nectar, and Ambrosia. Or, the bread of the mighty, sc. that mightily strengthened them.
Heb. meat taken in hunting; so called, because dainty as venison, or, quia semper ambulabant, et in via quasi eam venabantur, sc. Jos 1:11 (Aben Ezra).
paragraphs.anchor: He sent them meat to the full

paragraphs.text: Pergere, to go, to pass away, and to give place to the south wind.
paragraphs.anchor: He caused an east wind to blow

paragraphs.text: That it might bring in the quails. Now Pliny writeth (lib. 10, c. 23), that quails, though they love to fly with the wind, because of their heavy bodies and small strength, yet not with the south wind, because it is moist, and so more heavy than the north wind, which therefore they rather delight in. And if this be true, here is another miracle, saith an expositor, that these quails were brought in by that wind, which, when it bloweth, they commonly rest and hide themselves.
paragraphs.anchor: And by his power he brought in the south wind

paragraphs.text: Dapibus illos compluit. This he had done once before for them; see Exo 16:12-13, with Num 11:18-21; Num 11:31-33; their unbelief, therefore, and impatience this second time was the more heinous.
paragraphs.anchor: He rained flesh also upon them as dust

paragraphs.text: A day’s journey on each side, and about two cubits above the earth, Num 11:31, in such abundance, that Moses could not believe it were possible to be done, though all the fish in the sea should be gathered together, and turned into flesh, Num 11:31.
paragraphs.anchor: And he let it fall in the midst of their camp

paragraphs.text: But better they had fasted. Many eat that on earth which they must digest in hell; these here were murdering morsels.
paragraphs.anchor: So they did eat, and were well filled

paragraphs.text: They were heard, ad voluntatem, non ad utilitatem. Deus saepe dat iratus quod negat propitius. God’s gifts to a graceless man are giftless gifts; and he had better a great deal be without them.
paragraphs.anchor: He gave them their own desire

paragraphs.text: Satiated they were, but not satisfied. It is as easy to quench the fire of Aetna as the thoughts set on fire by lust.
paragraphs.anchor: They were not estranged from their lust

paragraphs.text: Heb. ascended, as a flame, which the bigger it groweth the higher it getteth.
paragraphs.anchor: The wrath of God came upon them

paragraphs.text: Those that had glutted and stuffed themselves like a woolpack, being nitida et bene curata cute pingues, fat and fair-liking.
paragraphs.anchor: And slew the fattest of them

paragraphs.text: Or, The young men, who by a hasty testament bequeathed that new name, Kibroth-hattaavah, that is, the graves of lust, to the place they lay buried In.
paragraphs.anchor: And smote down the chosen men of Israel

paragraphs.text: They utterly lost the fruit of their calamities; which godly men hold a very great loss.
paragraphs.anchor: For all this they sinned still

paragraphs.text: Neither mercies nor crosses duly affected them.
paragraphs.anchor: And believed not

paragraphs.text: So that they never saw the promised land, for the which they came out of Egypt; but their carcasses fell in the wilderness. Who knoweth, saith a reverend man, whether God purpose not to wear out this present generation that hath been defiled with the superstition of the world, that we may not see the good that he will bring upon this Church?
paragraphs.anchor: Therefore their days did he consume in vanity

paragraphs.text: Or, in terror, for they were in continual fear of God’s wrath, of their enemies round about, of wild beasts, fiery serpents, &c.
paragraphs.anchor: And their years in trouble

paragraphs.text: Fictis scilicet, quibusdam et fucatis pollicitationabus, with a few dissembled devotions.
paragraphs.anchor: When he slew them, then they sought him

paragraphs.text: So many now, when deadly, sick, will be wondrous good. Nuper me amici cuiusdam languor admonuit, optimos esse nos dum infirmi sumus (Plin. eph 26, 1. 7). As iron is very soft and malleable while in the fire, but soon after returneth to its former hardness; so many, while afflicted, seem very well affected, but afterwards soon show what they are. William Rufus, in a fit of sickness at Gloucester, vowed upon his recovery to see all vacancies in the Church furnished; which he did, but with so great ado as showed that, having escaped the danger, he would willingly have deceived the saint, saith the chronicler.

In the sweating sickness here in England, so long as the ferventness of the plague lasted there was crying, Peccavi, peccavi, I have sinned, I have sinned, the ministers were sought for in every corner, You must come to my lord, you must come to my lady, &c.; but this lasted with many little longer than the disease; so deceitful is man’s heart, and desperately wicked. Most men are nailed to the earth (saith one well), as Sisera was by Jael; and will not so much as lift up their eyes to heaven, unless it be as hogs do, who go noddling down and rooting in the earth all their life, and never look upward till, being ready to be killed, they are laid flat upon their backs and forced; so these, till wrestling with the pangs of death, they are fastened to their sick-beds, &c.
But they gave but the half turn, they turned not even unto God with all their heart, as Joe 2:12.
paragraphs.anchor: And they returned

paragraphs.text: Heb. Manicabant sive aurorizabant Deum, aurora velut anticipata; they were up and at it by peep of day.
paragraphs.anchor: And inquired early after God

paragraphs.text: Misery is the best art of memory. But this remembrance of God was but as letters written in the sand, or as a picture drawn on the ice, that long continueth not; it was but a flash, and while they were in a good mood; it was but as Nebuchadnezzar’s dream, which he had soon forgotten. They remembered God, lingua non corde, with the tongue, but not with the heart, as Aben Ezra here glosseth. They gave God a mess of fair words, calling him Rock, Redeemer, &c., but he is not to be so courted and complimented; goats may be fed with leaves, but God is not mocked.
paragraphs.anchor: And they remembered

paragraphs.text: They looked pitifully, as the fox caught in a gin doth, but it is only to get out; they spake God fair, as the devil in the Gospel did our Saviour, but it was only to be rid of him. They worshipped him, as the Indians do the devil, that he may do them no hurt. The Latin word Colo, to worship, is by some derived of the Greek word κολακευειν, to flatter, and the English word flatter, from the Greek λατρευειν, to worship. Sure it is that many men’s devotion is mere dissimulation.
paragraphs.anchor: Ver 36. Nevertheless they did flatter him with their mouth

paragraphs.text: sc. While they called him Rock, Redeemer, and all was but from the teeth outward; which how much God abhorreth as a ludibrious devotion, see Jer 3:4-5. And here it is said to be the middle of the psalter; for hitherto the Hebrews reckon one thousand two hundred sixty and three verses; and as many they note to be yet left in the second part.
paragraphs.anchor: And they lied unto him

paragraphs.text: It was still the old heart, without any sincere change, and that can never hold out the hardships of holiness, but will deviate and falsify; the rack may make it roar, the rod flutter, but all is in hypocrisy. A hypocrite would cozen God of heaven if he could tell how.
paragraphs.anchor: For their heart was not right with him

paragraphs.text: See Psa 78:8.
paragraphs.anchor: Neither were they steadfast

paragraphs.text: Not standing upon terms nor taking advantages; a sin pardoning God, whose mercy rejoiceth against (or glorieth over) judgment, Jas 2:13; it is of his mercy that we are not consumed, Lam 3:22, if he should deal with us in strict justice, Et delicta nostra ad calculos vocare, there were no abiding by it, Psal. cxxx. 1; clxiii 1.
paragraphs.anchor: But he, being full of compassion

paragraphs.text: With patience and piety, he overcame their provocations, although they tempted him ten times, that is, very often, Num 14:22.
paragraphs.anchor: Yea, many a time turned he his anger away

paragraphs.text: Heb. He multiplied to turn away his wrath, Strenue curavit ut cohiberet iram suam, he let fall some drops of his wrath, but would not shed the whole shower of it.
paragraphs.anchor: And did not stir up all his wrath

paragraphs.text: i.e. Frail and feeble, full of sin and misery., {see Gen 6:3} altogether unable to grapple with God’s wrath.
paragraphs.anchor: For he remembered that they were but flesh

paragraphs.text: Et in suis reciprocationibus evanescens. For winds neither return thither whence they blow, nor yet pass from one coast to another, but are wasted in the middle of the world, by the force of the sun and by their own motion, as Aristotle concludeth in his discourse concerning metaphors. Now, what is man (saith Nazianzen) but soul and soil, breath and body, a puff of wind the one, a pile of dust the other, no solidity in either?
paragraphs.anchor: A wind that passeth away, &c.

paragraphs.text: Exclamatio pathetica. Ten times at least in the first two years, Num 16:1-50; Num 17:1-13; Num 18:1-32; Num 19:1-22 What, then, in all the rest? Quis fando possit enarrare tot rebelliones. From the very day they came out of Egypt they were always contending against the Lord, as Moses telleth them, when he was taking his leave of them, Deu 31:16-18.
paragraphs.anchor: How oft did they provoke him in the wilderness

paragraphs.text: Where they were at his mercy, and at his immediate finding.
paragraphs.anchor: And grieve him in the desert

paragraphs.text: They did it afresh, and after some resolutions and short winded wishes of doing better.
paragraphs.anchor: Yea, they turned back and tempted God

paragraphs.text: Designarunt, they prescribed to him, and set him his bounds which he must not pass; as Popilius, the Roman ambassador, drew a circle round about King Antiochus, and bade him give answer ere he stirred out of it, for he would be put off no longer. Now, God is limited, when as either his power is questioned, as Psa 78:20, or his will circumscribed, as if he were bound to serve man’s lusts, or means appointed him whereby he must work, and not otherwise.
paragraphs.anchor: And limited the Holy One

paragraphs.text: Forgetfulness is the root of rebellion and of all vice, as the Genevists well note here. Eaten bread is soon forgotten, Nihil citius senescit quam gratia (Seneca).
paragraphs.anchor: They remembered not his hand

paragraphs.text: viz. From Pharaoh, but so soon as they had sucked the honey they despised the flower.
paragraphs.anchor: Nor the day when he delivered them

paragraphs.text: That stage of wonders. See Psa 78:12.
paragraphs.anchor: How he had wrought his signs in Egypt

paragraphs.text: A great city in Egypt, whereof read Isa 19:11; Isa 19:13; Isa 30:4 Eze 30:14. Josephus, Antiq. lib. 1, cap. 9. See Psa 78:12.
paragraphs.anchor: In the field of Zoan

paragraphs.text: Seven of those ten plagues of Egypt are here instanced, to aggravate the forgetfulness or perfidy of the Israelites. Good turns aggravate unkindness, and our offences are increased by our obligations.
paragraphs.anchor: And had turned their rivers into blood, &c.

paragraphs.text: Usque adeo ut aquae potabiles totam, alioqui stagnantem Aegyptum, deficerent. The Rabbis say (who told them I know not) that out of the same vessel an Egyptian drank blood and an Israelite water (Midras Tilling).
paragraphs.anchor: And their floods, that they could not drink

paragraphs.text: Miscellam muscarum venenatarum, venomous flies and flying serpents, whose poison and sting did even corrupt the land, Exo 8:24. The Greek rendereth it κυνομυιαν, the dog-fly.
paragraphs.anchor: He sent divers sorts of flies among them

paragraphs.text: Together with the grasshopper, Exo 10:12-15, God’s great army, Joe 2:11
paragraphs.anchor: He gave also their increase unto the caterpillar

paragraphs.text: i.e. The fruits of the earth, which they had laboured for; they lost both their husbandry and their harvest.
paragraphs.anchor: And their labour

paragraphs.text: Heb. He killed, Quia planta habet animam vegetativain, ut Job 14:8, saith Kimchi.
paragraphs.anchor: He destroyed their vines with hail

paragraphs.text: Or, with great hailstones mingled with fire, running along and catching, Exo 9:24. Confer Rev 16:21.
paragraphs.anchor: And their sycamores with frost

paragraphs.text: Moses saith men also, who were brained and burned by it.
paragraphs.anchor: He gave up their cattle also to the hail

paragraphs.text: i.e. Some messengers of his wrath and displeasure, whether good or evil angels it skills not.
paragraphs.anchor: By sending evil angels among them

paragraphs.text: Heb. He weighed a path, recompensing their unjust stiffness with his just judgments, and proceeding in his anger from lighter plagues to that heaviest of all the rest, the slaying of all the flower of Egypt in one night, Psa 78:51.
paragraphs.anchor: He made a way to his anger

paragraphs.text: Certo pestis genere perniciocissimo et acutissimo. The Rabbis say that in each house was a dead corpse, viz. the chieftain of the family, whether there were a firstborn in it or not, Exo 12:30.
paragraphs.anchor: And smote all the firstborn in Egypt

paragraphs.text: Who was the father of Mizraim, the founder of the Egyptians, Gen 10:6, who vainly boasted that they were αυτοχθονες, as ancient as their land. Herodotus, the author of that story, tells us also of a certain great town in Egypt called Chemmim, from Cham likely.
paragraphs.anchor: In the tabernacle of Ham

paragraphs.text: i.e. Tuto et lente, softly and safely, as Gen 33:13, tending them with all tenderness, and providing for their necessities.
paragraphs.anchor: But made his own people to go forth like sheep

paragraphs.text: Or, if they did, it was without cause, Cur enim metuat hominem homo in sinu Dei positus.
paragraphs.anchor: And he led them on safely, so that they feared not

paragraphs.text: i.e. Of Judea, which country he had consecrated to himself for the place and chief seat of religion; whence it is called, the holy land. It had been a loathsome land, Ezr 9:11, filled with filthiness from corner to corner, but now otherwise. How it was afterwards again polluted, see Isa 1:21-23.
paragraphs.anchor: And he brought them to the border of his sanctuary

paragraphs.text: Moriah, whereon stood the temple; or, to this mountainous country of Judea.
paragraphs.anchor: Even to this mountain

paragraphs.text: See Psa 44:3.
paragraphs.anchor: Which his right hand, &c.

paragraphs.text: i.e. In their sight, and for their sake.
paragraphs.anchor: He cast out the heathen also before them

paragraphs.text: Not a material line, but mathematical, saith an interpreter; whereby we may perceive that the way of making maps was anciently in use among the Hebrews (Geneb.).
paragraphs.anchor: He divided them an inheritance by line

paragraphs.text: Notwithstanding all their former provocations. "See that none render evil for evil to any man, but ever follow" (by God’s example) "that which is good, both among yourselves and toward all men," 1Th 5:15.
paragraphs.anchor: And made the tribes of Israel, &c.

paragraphs.text: Neither God’s judgments on their enemies nor his mercies to themselves could keep them within the bounds of obedience; but in a land of uprightness they would deal unjustly, and not behold the majesty of the Lord, Isa 26:10.
paragraphs.anchor: Yet they tempted and provoked, &c.

paragraphs.text: They had a kind of willingness and velleity, a kind of wambling, as one speaketh, but it boiled not up to the full height of resolution for God.

paragraphs.text: Non semper feriet quodcunque minabitur arcus; but a deceitful bow, that turneth back into belly, as we say, will be sure to deceive the archer, though he level his eye and his arrow never so directly to the mark, and think with himself to hit it. Lo, such a false rotten bow is man’s deceitful heart; and hence the arrows of his purposes and promises vanish oft in the air, as smoke.
